title: Introductions
description: Introduce yourself, say where you are from and what you do, and ask the other person the same.

guide.title: 'I am X' needs no verb
guide.text:
To say that one thing is another, Kannada simply puts the two side by side: ನಾನು ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿ (naanu vidyaarthi) is literally 'I student'. There is no word for 'am', 'is' or 'are' in this kind of sentence, and no word for 'a' or 'the'.

ನನ್ನ (nanna) is 'my' and ನಿಮ್ಮ (nimma) is 'your' (polite). So: nanna hesaru ... 'my name (is) ...'.

ಹೆಸರೇನು (hesarenu) is hesaru 'name' + enu 'what', fused: the final u of hesaru drops before the vowel. You can also say the two words separately: nimma hesaru enu?

guide.title: Where are you from? The endings -inda, -alli and -ge
guide.text:
Kannada has no separate words for 'from', 'in' and 'to'. They are endings on the noun: -inda 'from', -alli 'in', -ge or -kke 'to'. A linking sound is added where needed: amerika + inda = amerikadinda; bengalooru + alli = bengaloorinalli; illi 'here' + ge = illige 'to here'.

ನೀವು ಎಲ್ಲಿಯವರು? (neevu elliyavaru?) is the natural way to ask where someone is from: elli 'where' + -avaru 'person of'. The answer uses the same ending: ನಾನು ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನವನು (naanu bengaloorinavanu, said by a man) or ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನವಳು (bengaloorinavalu, said by a woman) - 'I am a Bengaluru person'. The simpler answer with -inda bandiddeeni ('I have come from ...') works for everyone.

ಊರು (ooru) means one's home town or native place; ನಿಮ್ಮ ಊರು ಯಾವುದು? is a favourite opening question.

examples.english: I am from America. (I have come from America.)
I live in Bengaluru. (I am in Bengaluru.)

guide.title: Introducing someone: the respectful plural
guide.text:
ಇವರು (ivaru) literally means 'these people', but it is the normal respectful way to point to one person: 'this gentleman / this lady'. The noun then also takes the plural ending -aru: snehita 'friend' becomes snehitaru. So ಇವರು ನನ್ನ ಸ್ನೇಹಿತರು can mean 'this is my friend' or 'these are my friends'.

Use ivaru for any adult you are introducing. The familiar forms ivanu (this boy/man) and ivalu (this girl/woman) are for children and close friends; they are taught in the unit on pronouns.

phrases.note: hesaru (name) + enu (what) join into one word. The e of -enu is long.
Replace 'raaj' with your own name. Kannada needs no word for 'is' here.
Literally 'You are a person of where?'
The ending -inda means 'from'. Written form of the verb: bandiddene (ಬಂದಿದ್ದೇನೆ).
A polite, slightly formal sentence. Both e in bheti and o in santosha are long.
Most modern job names are the English words.

phrases.english: I am here on a visit.
phrases.note: pravaasa = trip, tour; the ending -kke here means 'for'.
Spoken form; in writing: neevu elli vaasisutteeri? (ನೀವು ಎಲ್ಲಿ ವಾಸಿಸುತ್ತೀರಿ?)
The ending -alli means 'in'. In fast speech: bengalooralli (ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಲ್ಲಿ).
ooru is the place your family comes from, not just where you live now.
Written form: kaliyuttiddene (ಕಲಿಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದೇನೆ). People are delighted to hear this.
The plural form is used for one person to show respect.
